introduction-choosing-the-right-tool.core: Every data structure optimises some operations at the cost of others. Choosing well means listing the operations your problem needs most (lookup, insert, ordered iteration, min/max) and picking the structure that makes those cheap.

first_principles.problem: A candidate uses a list for membership checks inside a loop and gets O(n²).
truths: No structure is best at everything.

analogy.title: A toolbox
analogy.story: You don't use a hammer for screws; pick the tool for the job.
analogy.breaks: Tools don't interact; you often combine structures (hash map + linked list for LRU).

example.title: Designing an LRU cache
flow: Need O(1) recency reorder → doubly linked list
example.outcome: the right structure for the workload.

check.q: Which two structures make an O(1) LRU cache?
check.a: A hash map for lookup plus a doubly linked list for recency order.

arrays-speed-vs-flexibility.core: An array stores elements contiguously, so element i's address is base + i × size: O(1) random access and excellent cache locality. Inserting or deleting in the middle requires shifting elements (O(n)), and fixed arrays can't grow.

first_principles.problem: Frequent inserts at the front of a large array are surprisingly slow.

analogy.title: Houses on a numbered street
analogy.story: Find number 57 instantly, but inserting a new house between 12 and 13 means renumbering everyone after.
analogy.breaks: Real streets don't benefit from caching; arrays do, via CPU cache lines.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Match the structure to where you insert.

check.q: Why is array index access O(1)?
check.a: The address is computed directly as base + index × element size.

dynamic-arrays-how-resizing-works.core: Dynamic arrays (Python list, Java ArrayList, C++ vector) keep a capacity larger than their size. When full, they allocate a bigger block (typically ×1.5–2), copy elements and free the old one. Appends are O(1) amortised, with occasional O(n) spikes.

first_principles.problem: We need array speed without knowing the final size.
truths: Contiguous blocks can't grow in place reliably.

analogy.title: Moving to a bigger flat when you outgrow yours
analogy.story: Each move is a hassle, but you buy double the space so you move rarely.
analogy.breaks: Moving house takes days regardless; copying cost grows with how much you own.

check.q: What's the worst-case cost of a single append to a dynamic array?
check.a: O(n), when it triggers a resize and copy.

linked-lists-the-chain.core: A linked list stores nodes anywhere in memory, each pointing to the next (and previous, if doubly linked). Inserting or deleting at a known node is O(1), but finding the i-th element requires walking from the head (O(n)), and pointer chasing is cache-unfriendly.

first_principles.problem: We need O(1) removal of arbitrary known elements, which arrays can't do.
truths: Pointers decouple logical and physical order.
derivation: Use a **dummy head** to simplify edge cases.

analogy.title: A treasure hunt
analogy.story: Each clue tells you where the next one is; you can't jump to clue 7 without following 1 to 6.
analogy.breaks: Adding a clue in a real hunt means rewriting a clue, just as insertion rewires one pointer.

check.q: Why are linked lists slower than arrays for iteration in practice?
check.a: Nodes are scattered in memory, so traversal causes cache misses.

linked-list-algorithms-reversal.core: Reversing a singly linked list in place uses three pointers: prev, curr and next. For each node, save next, point curr.next back to prev, then advance prev and curr. It's O(n) time, O(1) space, and the building block for many list problems.

first_principles.problem: Candidates lose the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it.
truths: Each node must point to its predecessor.
Overwriting next loses the remaining chain.
derivation: Loop: **nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt**.

analogy.title: Turning around a conga line one person at a time
analogy.story: Each person turns to face the one who was behind them, while you keep hold of who's next.
analogy.breaks: People can see the whole line; your code sees only the pointers it saved.

code.text:
def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev, curr = curr, nxt
    return prev

check.q: What's returned as the new head?
check.a: prev, which points to the original tail after the loop.

cycle-detection-the-tortoise-and-the-har.core: Floyd's algorithm moves a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps. If there's a cycle, fast eventually laps slow and they meet; if fast hits null, there's no cycle. Resetting one pointer to head and moving both one step finds the cycle's start. O(n) time, O(1) space.

first_principles.problem: Detecting a loop in a linked list with a visited set costs O(n) memory.
truths: In a cycle, a faster runner catches a slower one.
The gap closes by one each step.
Meeting-point maths locates the cycle start.
derivation: **Reset** slow to head, step both by 1 → meet at start.

analogy.title: Two runners on a circular track
analogy.story: The faster runner always laps the slower one if the track loops.
analogy.breaks: Runners have continuous speed; pointers move in discrete steps, but the gap still closes by one each step.

check.q: Why are the slow and fast pointers guaranteed to meet in a cycle?
check.a: Inside the cycle the gap between them shrinks by one each step, so it must reach zero.

stacks-lifo.core: A stack is Last-In-First-Out: push and pop at the top in O(1). It models nested, 'most recent first' processing: function calls, undo history, bracket matching, DFS and monotonic-stack problems like 'next greater element'.

first_principles.problem: Validating nested brackets like {[()]} needs to remember the most recent unmatched opener.
truths: Nesting closes in reverse order of opening.
Only the top element matters next.
derivation: **Push** openers, **pop** on closers and check match.

analogy.title: A stack of plates
analogy.story: You add and take plates only from the top.
analogy.breaks: You can peek at a plate in the middle; a stack's interface forbids it.

steps.label: Trace
steps.detail: {[()]} → push { [ ( then pop in reverse → valid.

queues-fifo.core: A queue is First-In-First-Out: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front, both O(1) with a deque or ring buffer. Queues model fairness and level-by-level processing: BFS, task scheduling, rate limiting and producer-consumer buffers.

first_principles.problem: Using list.pop(0) as a queue in Python makes BFS O(n²).
truths: Arrival order should equal service order.
derivation: **BFS** with a queue for shortest unweighted paths.
**Priority queue** (heap) when order is by priority.

analogy.title: A queue at a coffee shop
analogy.story: First in line gets served first.
analogy.breaks: People can jump the line; a priority queue formalises that by priority.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: First arrival at goal is the shortest path.

check.q: Why does BFS find shortest paths in unweighted graphs?
check.a: The FIFO queue explores nodes in order of distance, so the first time you reach a node is via the fewest edges.

hashmaps-the-magic-lookup.core: A hash map runs a key through a hash function to get a bucket index, giving average O(1) insert, lookup and delete. It is the single most useful interview structure: counting, deduplication, two-sum complements, caching and grouping.

first_principles.problem: Finding pairs that sum to a target with nested loops is O(n²).
truths: A hash function turns keys into array indices.
Keys must be hashable and immutable.

analogy.title: A coat check
analogy.story: You hand over a coat, get ticket 47, and later go straight to hook 47.
analogy.breaks: Two coats never share a hook at a coat check, but hash maps must handle collisions.

check.q: Why can't lists be dictionary keys in Python?
check.a: They're mutable, so their hash could change after insertion and the entry would be lost.

hashmaps-collisions-resizing.core: Different keys can hash to the same bucket. Chaining stores a list per bucket; open addressing probes for another slot. As load factor (items ÷ buckets) rises, collisions grow, so the map resizes (typically doubling) and rehashes everything, keeping operations O(1) amortised. Bad hashes or adversarial keys degrade it to O(n).

first_principles.problem: A service slows to a crawl when attackers send many keys that collide (hash flooding).

analogy.title: Parking in a full car park
analogy.story: If your spot is taken you drive to the next free one, and when it's nearly full the operator builds a bigger car park.
analogy.breaks: Building a car park takes months; resizing is a single O(n) pause.

example.title: Load factor growth
example.outcome: fast maps under growth and attack.

check.q: What is a hash map's load factor?
check.a: The number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets.
